name: Acetyl tetrapeptide-5
route: Applied to the skin in eye creams and gels
status: Cosmetic ingredient; not an FDA-approved drug
mechanism: Proposed to ease eye-area puffiness by affecting the enzyme ACE and slowing glycation, based mainly on lab and manufacturer data

article.summary: Acetyl tetrapeptide-5 (Eyeseryl) is an eye-cream peptide marketed to reduce under-eye puffiness. No independent human trial of the peptide alone was found, so evidence is very limited.
article.takeaway: Acetyl tetrapeptide-5, sold as Eyeseryl, is a four-amino-acid peptide added to eye creams and gels to reduce puffiness and a tired look. It is proposed to work by affecting an enzyme called ACE and by limiting glycation, a sugar-driven stiffening of proteins, which together are thought to reduce fluid build-up around the eyes. In a 2021 study on cultured skin cells it was one of five peptides tested, and a mixture containing it lowered markers of oxidative damage,[^1] but **no independent human trial** of the peptide on its own turned up in the literature searched. Under-eye bags have several causes, some structural, that a cream cannot reach.
glance: Under-eye puffiness and a tired look
Eye creams and gels, once or twice daily
Signal peptide (proposed ACE and glycation effects)
Cell studies; no independent human trial found

blocks.text: The skin around the eyes is thin, so fluid and pigment show through easily. Morning puffiness can come from fluid pooling, while lasting under-eye bags are often caused by fat shifting forward as the supporting tissue loosens. A cream can at most address the first kind.

Acetyl tetrapeptide-5 is proposed to work in two ways: by interfering with angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE), which takes part in fluid and blood-vessel regulation, and by limiting glycation, the sugar-linked damage that stiffens collagen. The 2021 cell study used ACE1 activity as the measure when choosing this peptide's best concentration.[^1] What that means for puffiness in living people has not been shown.

rows: The best mixture (carnosine, acetyl tetrapeptide-5, hexapeptide-11 and acetyl hexapeptide-3) lowered oxidative damage markers and raised collagen and elastin markers after hydrogen peroxide stress[^1]
Controlled human trials of the peptide alone
None found in the peer-reviewed literature searched for this entry
Systematic review of anti-aging cosmetic ingredients (2021)
Good supporting data for many common ingredients are often missing[^2]

blocks.text: Results in a dish do not show whether a cream changes puffiness in people, and claims on product pages could not be checked against published trials.

It is formulated into eye creams, gels and roll-on serums, usually applied once or twice a day around the orbital bone. Keep products out of the eyes themselves. Any change would be judged after several weeks of use.

Eye-area skin is delicate and prone to irritation, and fragrance or preservatives in a formula are more common culprits than the peptide. No safety data specific to this peptide were found in the sources reviewed.
Cosmetics do not need FDA approval before sale, and products that claim to change how the body works can be treated as drugs.[^3]

Acetyl tetrapeptide-5 is a plausible but unproven eye-cream ingredient. For persistent or structural under-eye bags, a dermatologist or oculoplastic surgeon can explain options that a cream cannot match.

evidence.label: Very limited: cell studies only
evidence.text: The published work on this peptide is a cell study of mixtures,[^1] with no independent human trial located. Reviews of cosmetic anti-aging ingredients stress that supporting data are often lacking.[^2]

faq.q: Does acetyl tetrapeptide-5 get rid of eye bags?
faq.a: There is no verified evidence that it does. Puffiness has several causes, and fat that has shifted forward under the eye is beyond the reach of a cream.
Eyeseryl is a trade name for an ingredient whose active peptide is acetyl tetrapeptide-5, supplied to cosmetic makers for eye-area products.

faq.q: Does combining peptides in one product help?
faq.a: Not necessarily. The 2021 study noted that peptide combinations can act in synergistic or opposing ways, so each formula needs its own testing.[^1]
